transcript.speaker: Sophia James
transcript.content: I totally get being hesitant — adopting is a real commitment and you’re smart to think it through. Consider easing in: foster a pet first or adopt an older, lower-energy dog or a cat, and use services like training classes, a pet sitter, or dog-walking apps so it doesn’t all fall on you. I’m happy to help with walks or basic training and to visit the shelter with you — pets give steady companionship and routine that can really help with loneliness, and shelters often offer follow-up support so you won’t be doing it alone.

transcript.speaker: Eli Dawson
transcript.content: You're right — fostering or adopting an older, low-energy pet is a sensible way to ease into this. Ask the shelter staff to give them time and follow-up support so the adoption isn’t rushed; many people do best with a gradual transition. I can come with you to the shelter or help with initial walks and basic training when they’re ready.

transcript.speaker: Sophia James
transcript.content: Totally — maybe start by asking them what their biggest worry is (time, cost, future moves, allergies), so we can address it specifically. We could set up a 30‑day foster trial with a clear daily routine, a simple budget and a sitter/training backup; I’ll help map that plan and be available for walks or check‑ins so they don’t feel like they’re doing it alone.

transcript.speaker: Eli Dawson
transcript.content: Good — asking about their biggest worry and offering a 30‑day foster trial is exactly the gradual approach that will help someone feel safe making this change. I’ll contact the shelter to discuss arranging the trial and what follow‑up support they provide, and I’ll come with them to the visit; I’m also happy to help draft a simple daily routine and budget and to assist with initial walks and basic training. We’ll keep this patient and reversible — with clear expectations and a little backup, they’ll be in a much better position to choose confidently.
